slides.page_title: 10 Database Concepts for System Design Interviews

cover.title: 10 Database Concepts
cover.subtitle: You Can’t Skip in System Design Interviews
cover.tagline: Ordered from foundational to advanced, each with a worked example, its trade-offs and the interview takeaway.

items: A separate ==sorted structure==, usually a **B-tree**
Maps column values to row locations
Point and range lookups become a few page reads
`WHERE email = 'a@x.com'` scans all 10M rows: __O(n)__
A B-tree lookup is __O(log n)__
That is about **3-4** page reads
`WHERE` filters and `JOIN` keys
`ORDER BY` without a separate sort
`UNIQUE` constraints and foreign keys
Point and range lookups skip the linear scan
==Covering index== holds every needed column: index-only scan
`UNIQUE` index enforces uniqueness cheaply
Each write also updates **every** index: slower `INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE`, more disk
Indexing low-cardinality columns (boolean, status) rarely helps
`LOWER(email)` wraps the column and bypasses the index

blocks.title: Interview takeaway
blocks.text: Index what you filter, join and sort on, equality columns first, and verify with EXPLAIN. Indexes trade write cost for read speed.
A __transaction__ bundles many statements into one ==all-or-nothing== unit, so a crash never leaves data half-done.
A group of reads and writes the database treats as **one** logical unit. It either fully {green:commits} or fully {red:rolls back}.

items: A crash midway through a multi-step change leaves data half-updated
Debit done, credit lost: $100 simply vanishes
Money transfers between accounts
Order placement plus stock decrement
Any ==multi-row invariant==
Example : move $100 from account 1 to 2
2nd UPDATE fails: `ROLLBACK` restores **both** rows
Under the hood a ==WAL== logs changes before applying them
So a commit survives a crash
No partial failures, because the unit is {green:atomic}
Code reasons about state __before__ and __after__ only
`SAVEPOINT` allows partial rollback inside a long transaction
Long transactions hold locks and bloat the log: keep them short
Never wait on user input or a remote API inside one
Covers a **single** database only; across services use sagas or 2PC

blocks.title: Interview takeaway
blocks.text: Wrap multi-step invariants in a transaction, keep it short, and know it stops at the database boundary.
==ACID== = Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability: the four guarantees of a reliable __transaction__.

items: A predictable contract for developers
Correctness never depends on **timing** or crashes
Used for payments, inventory, bookings
Any system where wrong data costs money
**A**: second UPDATE fails, so ROLLBACK restores both
**C**: A going below 0 violates CHECK, aborts
**I**: others never see A debited, B not credited
**D**: once COMMIT returns, a crash cannot lose it

blocks.title: Recovery
blocks.text: After a crash, the database replays the ==WAL== to a known good state.

items: Strong correctness on a **single node**
Simpler app code: the DB enforces invariants
Crash recovery replays the WAL
Rollback uses undo; durability uses WAL
ACID 'C' (constraints hold) is not CAP 'C' (replicas agree)
Strict isolation and fsync per commit cost throughput
Many NoSQL stores relax ACID (BASE) to scale

blocks.title: Interview takeaway
blocks.text: Give a one-line example per letter, and say ==Isolation== is the tunable one.

items: ==Isolation level== = which effects of concurrent transactions you may see
Why: full __serializability__ is slow, so you trade strictness for throughput
Chosen **per transaction**: READ COMMITTED for web requests
SERIALIZABLE for financial ledgers
==Dirty read==: you see **uncommitted** data
==Non-repeatable read==: same row changes between two reads
==Phantom read==: a new row appears in a repeated range query
Benefit: ==tune each workload==, correctness vs concurrency
Higher levels abort or block: ==retry== error `40001`
Write skew: two doctors both go off-call
It slips past Repeatable Read and snapshot isolation
Fix it with **Serializable** or explicit locks

blocks.title: See also
blocks.text: Snapshots come from MVCC (page 7); explicit locks are page 6.

blocks.title: Interview takeaway
blocks.text: Name the 3 anomalies, map them to the 4 levels, and say your database's default.

items: ==Lock==: a transaction claims a row, page or table; conflicting access **waits**
Why: two transactions updating one row at once cause ==lost updates==
Used for: inventory counts, seat bookings, balance updates, queue-claiming jobs
Pessimistic: ==exclusive access== to a critical row, no lost updates
Optimistic: **no waiting**, suits low-contention workloads
__Deadlock__: T1 waits for T2, T2 waits for T1; DB kills one victim
Fix: take locks in a ==consistent order==, then retry the victim
Lock escalation and long-held locks cut concurrency
Job queues: `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` skips rows already claimed

blocks.title: Interview takeaway
blocks.text: High contention: pessimistic locks. Low contention: optimistic versioning. Always mention deadlock handling.
==MVCC== keeps **several versions** of a row, and each transaction reads one consistent __snapshot__.

items: Plain locking: readers block writers
Writers also block readers
Throughput collapses under mixed load
Snapshots remove the read-write wait
{icon:postgresql} PostgreSQL, {icon:mysql} MySQL InnoDB, Oracle
Snapshot reads under Read Committed and Repeatable Read
UPDATE never overwrites; it adds a new version
Version tagged with txid (Postgres `xmin`/`xmax`)
Reader at txid 100 sees only older commits

blocks.title: Why T1 still sees 10
blocks.text: Version 12 is newer than T1's snapshot, so it stays invisible.

items: Readers never block writers
Writers never block readers
Repeatable reads with no read locks
Long reports run on a stable snapshot
Old versions pile up as dead rows
Postgres needs `VACUUM`; InnoDB purges undo log
Long transactions stop that cleanup
Writers still conflict and take row locks
Snapshot isolation allows **write skew**

blocks.title: Interview takeaway
blocks.text: MVCC trades extra storage and cleanup work for non-blocking reads. That is why Postgres read-heavy workloads scale.
A ==connection pool== is a cache of open database connections. The app __borrows__ one, runs its query and **returns** it, instead of opening a new one per request.

items: New connection = TCP + TLS + auth, tens of ms
Each one costs a server process or thread
Postgres spends about ==10MB== per connection
Opening one per request wastes time and RAM
Web backends
Serverless functions
Any service with many short queries

blocks.title: pgbouncer modes
blocks.text: Transaction mode hands out a connection only for the length of one transaction.

items: Removes setup latency from the request path
Caps connections: Postgres `max_connections` defaults to ==100==
Backpressure: excess requests __queue__, not crash the DB
Pool too big causes **contention**
Pool too small causes timeouts
Start near (cores x 2) + disks
Leaked connections drain the pool
`SET` and prepared statements break in transaction mode

blocks.title: Interview takeaway
blocks.text: The database has a connection limit, so put a pool or proxy in front and size it deliberately, especially with serverless or many app instances.
==Partitioning== splits one logical table into smaller __physical partitions__ inside **one** database server.

items: A 2-billion-row table makes indexes slow and unwieldy
VACUUM crawls over the whole table
Big `DELETE`s rewrite millions of rows
{icon:postgresql} Time-series and log tables
Multi-tenant tables, one slice per tenant
Archiving old data cheaply
Pruning: queries touch only the relevant partition
`DROP TABLE orders_2025_01` is **instant**; `DELETE` of millions is not
Smaller per-partition indexes fit in memory
No filter on the partition key: scans **every** partition
Bad key gives hot partitions: everyone writes to this month
Unique constraints must include the partition key

blocks.title: Not sharding
blocks.text: Partitioning organizes rows on a single node (a split by rows) and adds no machines; sharding does that.

items: ==Replication== = continuously copying data from a primary node to replicas
Why: one node is a __single point of failure__ and a read bottleneck
Used for: HA failover, read scaling, geo-local reads, backups
App writes to the **primary**; it appends to its WAL / binlog
The log is streamed to every replica, which replays it
Reads go to replicas: 1 primary + 3 replicas serve 80% reads

blocks.note: replica lag returns the old value

blocks.text: Fix: ==read-your-writes==. Route that user's reads to the **primary** for a short window after their write.

items: Reading a replica right after a write: stale data
Expecting more replicas to add **write** capacity
Two nodes both acting as primary: split-brain
Automatic failover keeps service up when the primary dies
Add replicas to scale read throughput

blocks.title: Interview takeaway
blocks.text: Replication gives availability and read scale, not write scale. State sync versus async, then the lag problem.

items: ==Sharding== splits rows across independent database servers
Each shard owns a **subset** of the rows
One machine can't hold the data or the writes, so scale out
Used for social feeds, messaging and e-commerce at 100M+ users

blocks.note: same key always lands on same shard

blocks.text: ==Consistent hashing== moves only ~1/N of keys when a shard is added. Plain `% N` going 4 to 5 would move about **80%**.

items: Write and storage capacity scale almost **linearly**
Smaller dataset per node means faster queries
Fault isolation: one shard down, others keep serving
Cross-shard joins and transactions: slow or unsupported
Query without the shard key hits **every** shard
Hot key: one celebrity user overloads a single shard
Resharding live data is painful

blocks.title: Shard last
blocks.text: Exhaust indexing, caching, replication and partitioning first. Then pick the shard key by access pattern.

rows: leftmost prefix; slower writes, more space
FOR UPDATE vs version column; deadlocks
readers never block writers; needs VACUUM
range, list or hash, one server
sync safe but slow; async fast, lossy; lag = stale reads
split by shard key, many servers

items: Replicas add read capacity, not write capacity
A partitioned table still lives on one server
Say the shard key before you say "shard"

blocks.title: Key rule
blocks.text: Replication ==copies==, partitioning and sharding ==split==. Only sharding splits across servers.

caption.text:
10 database concepts that separate a pass from a "we'll be in touch" in system design interviews. 🗄️

You can know every box-and-arrow diagram, but the moment the interviewer asks "what happens when two writes collide?", shallow database knowledge gets exposed fast. These 10 come up again and again, and you need to explain each one: how it works, what it costs, and when to pick it.

1. Indexing
2. Transactions
3. ACID
4. Isolation Levels
5. Locking
6. MVCC
7. Connection Pooling
8. Partitioning
9. Replication
10. Sharding

Every page in the carousel has a worked example, the trade-offs, and the one-line interview takeaway. The last slide is a cheatsheet you can screenshot and revise from.

Which one confuses you most? Isolation levels? MVCC? Tell me below 👇

Comment “database” and save this for your next interview.
